transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Solving quadratic equations}\par Factorisation, the quadratic formula and substitution.
\textbf{2. Completing the square}\par Rewriting and solving quadratic expressions and equations.
\textbf{3. Quadratics as functions}\par Inputs, outputs, roots and minimum values.
\textbf{4. Quadratic graphs}\par Intercepts, turning points and equations from graphs.
\textbf{5. The discriminant}\par How many real roots?
\textbf{6. Modelling with quadratics}\par Using and interpreting quadratic models.

slides.title: Why do we care about quadratics…

transcription.tex: Quadratic relationships arise in many practical situations.

\textbf{Summations}\[1+2+\cdots+n=\frac12n^2+\frac12n\]A sports event awards 8 points, then 7, then 6, and so on. For \(1\le n\le8\) competitors:\[8+7+\cdots+(9-n)=\frac{n(17-n)}2\]The totals for one, two and three competitors are 8, 15 and 21.

\textbf{Projectile motion}\par Under constant acceleration,\[s=ut+\frac12at^2\]Here \(s\) is displacement, \(u\) initial velocity, \(a\) acceleration and \(t\) time. The expression is quadratic in \(t\).\par A projectile moving under gravity alone follows a parabolic path.

transcription.tex: Solve \(x^2+5x=6\). Two methods are shown below; completing the square is a third method.
\textbf{1. Factorisation}\quad First put the equation in the form \(ax^2+bx+c=0\).
\[\begin{aligned}x^2+5x-6&=0\\(x+6)(x-1)&=0\\x&=-6\text{ or }1\end{aligned}\]If a product is zero, at least one factor is zero.

transcription.tex: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic as \(a(x+b)^2+c\). The variable then appears only once, making several tasks easier.
\textbf{Sketching}\par The graph of \(y=(x+a)^2+b\) has minimum point \((-a,b)\).
\textbf{Later integration}\par In Further Maths, rewriting \(x^2-4x+5=(x-2)^2+1\) helps when integrating\[\int\frac1{x^2-4x+5}\,dx\]

transcription.tex: A function gives a rule that assigns one output to each permitted input. It is a formal version of a number machine.\[\text{input }x\quad\longrightarrow\quad f\quad\longrightarrow\quad\text{output }f(x)\]
\textbf{Example}\quad The function doubles its input. Write its rule.
\[f(x)=2x\]\(f\) is the name of the function; \(f(x)\) is its output for input \(x\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: For \(f(x)=x^2\), example inputs and outputs are:\[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}x&-1&0&1.7&2&3.1\\\hline f(x)&1&0&2.89&4&9.61\end{array}\]
\textbf{Domain and range}\quad What do these terms mean?
The domain is the set of permitted inputs. The range is the set of outputs achieved.\par With domain \(x\in\mathbb R\), the function \(f(x)=x^2\) has range \(f(x)\ge0\).
\textbf{Roots}\quad What is a root (or zero) of a function?
A value of \(x\) for which \(f(x)=0\).\par For \(f(x)=x^2\), the only root is \(x=0\).
\(x\in\mathbb R\) reads: \(x\) is a member of the set of real numbers.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Sketching a quadratic}\par Find and label the key features. A sketch does not require a uniform numerical scale.
\textbf{1. Roots}\par Solve \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) to find any \(x\)-intercepts.\par \textbf{2. Vertical intercept}\par Put \(x=0\): the point is \((0,c)\).
\textbf{3. Shape}\par If \(a>0\), the parabola opens upwards. If \(a<0\), it opens downwards.\par \textbf{4. Turning point}\par Complete the square: \(y=a(x-h)^2+k\) has turning point \((h,k)\).
The axis of symmetry is \(x=h\). Draw a smooth curve through the labelled points.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Why say “equal roots”?}\[x^2-12x+36=(x-6)^2\]The root 6 occurs twice as a factor. There is one distinct root, with multiplicity 2.

\textbf{Fundamental theorem of algebra}\par Every polynomial of degree \(n\ge1\) has exactly \(n\) complex roots when counted with multiplicity.\par The degree is the highest power with a nonzero coefficient. A quadratic has degree 2.\par Thus a quadratic always has two complex roots counting multiplicity, even when it has no real roots.

\textbf{An example of factorisation over the reals}\[\begin{aligned}x^4+a^4&=(x^2+\sqrt2ax+a^2)\\&\quad\times(x^2-\sqrt2ax+a^2)\end{aligned}\]Expanding gives \((x^2+a^2)^2-2a^2x^2=x^4+a^4\).\par Every real polynomial can be factored into real linear and quadratic factors.

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. MAT 2011 1B}\quad A rectangle has perimeter \(P\) and area \(A\). Which must hold?\[P^3>A;\quad A^2>2P+1;\quad P^2\ge16A;\quad PA>A+P\]
With side lengths \(x,y>0\), \(A=xy\) and \(P=2x+2y\).\[2x^2-Px+2A=0\]Real side lengths require \(P^2-16A\ge0\). Thus \(P^2\ge16A\).
\textbf{2. MAT 2006 1B}\quad How many real roots does \((2+x-x^2)^2=16\) have?
Consider \(2+x-x^2=4\) and \(2+x-x^2=-4\).\par The first gives \(x^2-x+2=0\), with negative discriminant. The second gives \((x+2)(x-3)=0\).\par Two distinct real roots: \(-2,3\).
\textbf{3. MAT 2009 1C}\quad For which real \(c\) does \(x^4=(x-c)^2\) have four real roots, counting repetitions?
The factors give \(x^2-x+c=0\) and \(x^2+x-c=0\). Both need nonnegative discriminants:\[1-4c\ge0,\quad1+4c\ge0\quad\Rightarrow\quad-\frac14\le c\le\frac14\]

transcription.tex: A spear is thrown from a tower over level ground. Its height in metres after \(t\) seconds is modelled by\[h(t)=12.25+14.7t-4.9t^2,\quad t\ge0\]A mathematical model describes a situation using simplifying assumptions.
The initial height is \(h(0)=12.25\) m: the height of the tower.
\textbf{(b)}\quad When does the spear hit the ground?
Solve \(h(t)=0\): \(t\approx-0.679\) or \(3.68\).\par Reject the negative time; the spear lands after 3.68 s (3 s.f.).
\textbf{(d)}\quad Find the maximum height and when it is reached.
The maximum height is 23.275 m, reached 1.5 s after release.

transcription.tex: A car model predicts fuel economy \(y\) mpg at speed \(x\) mph:\[y=-0.01x^2+0.975x+16,\quad x>0\]
\textbf{(a)}\quad Find the two speeds giving 32.5 mpg.
\textbf{(c)}\quad At what speed is fuel economy greatest?
At \(x=48.75\) mph, the squared term is zero and \(y\) is greatest.
\textbf{(d)}\quad Calculate the prediction at 120 mph and comment on validity.
\[y=-0.01(120)^2+0.975(120)+16=-11\]Negative mpg is impossible. The model is not valid at very high speeds.

transcription.tex: Grain yield \(g\), in tonnes per hectare, is modelled using fertiliser \(f\), in kilograms per hectare:\[g=6+0.03f-0.00006f^2\]
At \(f=0\), the yield is 6 tonnes per hectare.
\textbf{(b)}\quad A farmer currently uses 20 kg per hectare. Find the smallest additional amount needed to increase yield by 1 tonne per hectare.
\[\begin{aligned}g(20)&=6.576\\6+0.03f-0.00006f^2&=7.576\\f&\approx59.6\text{ or }440.4\end{aligned}\]The smaller increase is \(59.6-20=39.6\) kg per hectare (1 d.p.).

slides.title: Would you like $1,000,000 for finding roots?

transcription.tex: Roots are inputs that give an output of zero. Finding roots can also lead to major research problems.\par For real \(s>1\), the Riemann zeta function can be defined by\[\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^s}\]\[\zeta(2)=1+\frac1{2^2}+\frac1{3^2}+\cdots\]The function extends to complex inputs through a more advanced definition.

\textbf{The Riemann hypothesis}\par It predicts that every nontrivial zero of the extended zeta function has real part \(1/2\).\par This is a Millennium Prize Problem with a US$1 million prize for a qualifying solution. It connects zeros of a function with the distribution of prime numbers.
Read the Clay Mathematics Institute explanation
